items.title: Introduction

sections.normalized_html: A literal is a variable or a negation of a variable in a Boolean expression. For example, the following are all literals: [MATH: x, \quad y, \quad \overline{x}, \quad \overline{y}] Note that [MATH: \overline{x}] is the same as [MATH: \lnot\,x.] In contrast, the following are not literals: [MATH: \overline{\overline{x}}, \qquad x \land y, \qquad x \lor y, \qquad x \mid x]
sections.readable_text:
A literal is a variable or a negation of a variable in a Boolean expression. For example, the following are all literals:
[MATH: x, \quad y, \quad \overline{x}, \quad \overline{y}]
Note that [MATH: \overline{x}] is the same as [MATH: \lnot\,x.] In contrast, the following are not literals:
[MATH: \overline{\overline{x}}, \qquad x \land y, \qquad x \lor y, \qquad x \mid x]

An elementary disjunction is a disjunction of one or more literals. Some examples are as follows:
[MATH: x, \qquad \overline{y}, \qquad x \lor y, \qquad \overline{x} \lor y \lor \overline{z}]

sections.normalized_html: A formula is in conjunctive normal form (CNF) if it is a conjunction of one or more elementary disjunctions. For instance, [MATH: x, \qquad x \land \overline{y}, \qquad x \lor y, \qquad x \land (\overline{y} \lor z),\qquad (x \lor y) \land ({y} \lor \overline{z} \lor k)] are all in CNF. In contrast, the following expressions are not in CNF: [MATH: x \Rightarrow y, \qquad \overline{x \land y}, \qquad x \land \overline{(y \lor z)}, \qquad x\land (y \lor (z\land k))]

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following statements is true?

  1. [MATH: \overline{Y}] is a literal

  2. [MATH: Y \lor \overline{X}] is an elementary disjunction

  3. [MATH: (Y \lor \overline{X}) \land \overline{Z}] is a conjunctive normal form

Which of the following statements is true?

1. [MATH: \overline{Y}] is a literal
2. [MATH: Y \lor \overline{X}] is an elementary disjunction
3. [MATH: (Y \lor \overline{X}) \land \overline{Z}] is a conjunctive normal form

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that a literal is a variable or a negation of a variable, and an elementary disjunction is a disjunction of one or more literals.

A formula is in conjunctive normal form (CNF) if it is a conjunction of one or more elementary disjunctions. Also, [MATH: \overline{A}] means the same as [MATH: \lnot A.]

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, [MATH: Y] is a variable, and [MATH: \overline Y] is the negation of the variable. So, it's a literal.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, [MATH: Y \lor \overline{X}] is a disjunction of one or more literals.

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, [MATH: (Y \lor \overline{X})] and [MATH: \overline{Z}] are disjunctions of one or more literals. Our formula contains a conjunction of these elementary disjunctions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

To write a given Boolean function in conjunctive normal form,

- we eliminate all instances of logical operations other than [MATH: \lnot, \land, \lor,] then
- we rewrite the expression as a conjunction of elementary disjunctions.

Content:
For example, let's deduce a conjunctive normal form of [MATH: (\overline{x_3} \Rightarrow x_2) \land (x_1 \Rightarrow x_2).]

Content:
- First, using the fact that [MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \overline{A} \lor B,] we eliminate [MATH: \Rightarrow] from the expression:

- Then, we simplify the expression by applying the laws of logic:
[MATH: (\overline{\overline{x_3}} \lor x_2) \land (\overline{x_1} \lor x_2) \equiv (x_3 \lor x_2) \land ( \overline{x_1} \lor x_2)]

[MATH: (\overline{x_3} \Rightarrow x_2) \land (x_1 \Rightarrow x_2) \equiv (x_3 \lor x_2) \land ( \overline{x_1} \lor x_2),]
where the expression on the right-hand side is in conjunctive normal form.

items.title: Completing a Derivation of a Conjunctive Normal Form

sections.normalized_html: Complete the derivation of a disjunctive normal form below. [MATH: x_{3}^(―)⇒(x_{1}⊕x_{2})|≡; x 2∨(x_{1}⊕x_{2})|≡; x 2∨(x_{1}⊕x_{2})|≡; x 2∨((x 2∨x_{2})∧(x_{1}^(―)∨x 2))|≡; (x 2∨x_{2}∨x 2)∧(x_{1}^(―)∨x 2∨x_{3})]
EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
In general, to write down a formula in conjunctive normal form,

  • We eliminate all instances of logical operations other than [MATH: \overline{}, \land, \lor,] then

  • we rewrite the expression as a conjunction of elementary disjunctions.

In this example, we proceed as follows:

  • First, we use the fact that [MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \overline{A} \lor B] to eliminate [MATH: \Rightarrow] from the expression: [MATH: \overline{x_3} \Rightarrow (x_1 \oplus x_2) \equiv \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\overline{\overline{x_3}}} \lor (x_1 \oplus x_2)]

  • Then, we use [MATH: \overline{\overline{A}} \equiv A] to simplify the double negation: [MATH: \overline{\overline{x_3}} \lor (x_1 \oplus x_2) \equiv \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}x_3} \lor (x_1 \oplus x_2)]

  • Next, we use the fact that [MATH: A \oplus B \equiv (A \lor B) \land (\overline{A} \lor \overline{B})] to eliminate [MATH: \oplus] from the expression: [MATH: x_{3}∨(x_{1}⊕x_{2})|≡x 3∨((x 1∨x_{2})∧(x_{1}^(―)∨x 2 ―))]

  • Finally, we distribute the disjunction over the conjunction: [MATH: x_3 \lor (( x_1 \lor x_2) \land (\overline{x_1} \lor \overline{x_2})) \equiv (\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}x_1} \lor x_2 \lor \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}x_3}) \land (\overline{x_1} \lor \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\overline{x_2}} \lor x_3)]

Notice that the final expression is a conjunction of one or more elementary disjunctions. Therefore, this is a conjunctive normal form.

Recall the following logical equivalences:

[MATH: A⇒B|≡A^(―)∨B; A⇔B|≡(A^(―)∨B)∧(A∨B^(―)); A⊕B|≡(A∨B)∧(A^(―)∨B^(―))]

With that in mind, let's find an equivalent disjunctive normal form for the given formula.

  • First, we eliminate [MATH: \Rightarrow] and [MATH: \oplus] from the expression: [MATH: x_{1}⇒(x_{1}^(―)⊕x_{2})|≡; x_{1}^(―)∨(x_{1}^(―)⊕x_{2})|≡; x_{1}^(―)∨((x_{1}^(―)∨x_{2})∧(x_{1}^(―)^(―)∨x_{2}^(―)))]

  • Finally, we use the laws of logic to simplify the expression: [MATH: x_{1}^(―)∨((x_{1}^(―)∨x_{2})∧(x_{1}^(―)^(―)∨x_{2}^(―)))|≡; x_{1}^(―)∨((x_{1}^(―)∨x_{2})∧(x_{1}∨x_{2}^(―)))|≡; (x_{1}^(―)∨x_{1}^(―)∨x_{2})∧(x_{1}^(―)∨x_{1}∨x_{2}^(―))|≡; (x_{1}^(―)∨x_{2})∧(t∨x_{2}^(―))|≡; (x_{1}^(―)∨x_{2})∧t|≡; x_{1}^(―)∨x_{2}]

Our final expression is in conjunctive normal form.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A literal is a variable or a negation of a variable in a Boolean expression. For example, the following are all literals:
[MATH: x, \quad y, \quad \overline{x}, \quad \overline{y}]
Note that [MATH: \overline{x}] is the same as [MATH: \lnot\,x.] In contrast, the following are not literals:
[MATH: \overline{\overline{x}}, \qquad x \land y, \qquad x \lor y, \qquad x \mid x]

Content:
An elementary disjunction is a disjunction of one or more literals. Some examples are as follows:
[MATH: x, \qquad \overline{y}, \qquad x \lor y, \qquad \overline{x} \lor y \lor \overline{z}]

Content:
A formula is in conjunctive normal form (CNF) if it is a conjunction of one or more elementary disjunctions. For instance,
[MATH: x, \qquad x \land \overline{y}, \qquad x \lor y, \qquad x \land (\overline{y} \lor z),\qquad (x \lor y) \land ({y} \lor \overline{z} \lor k)]
are all in CNF.
In contrast, the following expressions are not in CNF:
[MATH: x \Rightarrow y, \qquad \overline{x \land y}, \qquad x \land \overline{(y \lor z)}, \qquad x\land (y \lor (z\land k))]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Conjunctive Normal Forms

Example Prompt:
Which of the following statements is true?

1. [MATH: \overline{Y}] is a literal
2. [MATH: Y \lor \overline{X}] is an elementary disjunction
3. [MATH: (Y \lor \overline{X}) \land \overline{Z}] is a conjunctive normal form

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that a literal is a variable or a negation of a variable, and an elementary disjunction is a disjunction of one or more literals.

A formula is in conjunctive normal form (CNF) if it is a conjunction of one or more elementary disjunctions. Also, [MATH: \overline{A}] means the same as [MATH: \lnot A.]

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, [MATH: Y] is a variable, and [MATH: \overline Y] is the negation of the variable. So, it's a literal.
- Statement II is true. Indeed, [MATH: Y \lor \overline{X}] is a disjunction of one or more literals.
- Statement III is true. Indeed, [MATH: (Y \lor \overline{X})] and [MATH: \overline{Z}] are disjunctions of one or more literals. Our formula contains a conjunction of these elementary disjunctions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

Item 5 — Tutorial: Conjunctive Normal Forms of a Function

Content:
Every Boolean function can be expressed in an equivalent conjunctive normal form (CNF).
In other words, for any Boolean function [MATH: f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n),] there exists an expression [MATH: C(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)] in CNF such that
[MATH: f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n) \equiv C(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n).]

Content:
To write a given Boolean function in conjunctive normal form,

Content:
- we eliminate all instances of logical operations other than [MATH: \lnot, \land, \lor,] then
- we rewrite the expression as a conjunction of elementary disjunctions.

Content:
For example, let's deduce a conjunctive normal form of [MATH: (\overline{x_3} \Rightarrow x_2) \land (x_1 \Rightarrow x_2).]

Content:
- First, using the fact that [MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \overline{A} \lor B,] we eliminate [MATH: \Rightarrow] from the expression:

Content:
[MATH: (x_{3}^(―)⇒x_{2})∧(x_{1}⇒x_{2})|≡(x_{3}^(―)^(―)∨x_{2})∧(x_{1}⇒x_{2}); ≡(x_{3}^(―)^(―)∨x_{2})∧(x_{1}^(―)∨x_{2})]

Content:
- Then, we simplify the expression by applying the laws of logic:
[MATH: (\overline{\overline{x_3}} \lor x_2) \land (\overline{x_1} \lor x_2) \equiv (x_3 \lor x_2) \land ( \overline{x_1} \lor x_2)]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that
[MATH: (\overline{x_3} \Rightarrow x_2) \land (x_1 \Rightarrow x_2) \equiv (x_3 \lor x_2) \land ( \overline{x_1} \lor x_2),]
where the expression on the right-hand side is in conjunctive normal form.

Content:
In this example, we used the fact that [MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \overline{A} \lor B.] Some logical equivalences we might use when writing a formula in CNF are

Content:
[MATH: A⇒B|≡A^(―)∨B,; A⇔B|≡(A^(―)∨B)∧(A∨B^(―)),; A⊕B|≡(A∨B)∧(A^(―)∨B^(―)).]

---

Item 6 — Example: Completing a Derivation of a Conjunctive Normal Form

Example Prompt:
Complete the derivation of a disjunctive normal form below.
[MATH: x_{3}^(―)⇒(x_{1}⊕x_{2})|≡; x 2∨(x_{1}⊕x_{2})|≡; x 2∨(x_{1}⊕x_{2})|≡; x 2∨((x 2∨x_{2})∧(x_{1}^(―)∨x 2))|≡; (x 2∨x_{2}∨x 2)∧(x_{1}^(―)∨x 2∨x_{3})]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
In general, to write down a formula in conjunctive normal form,

- We eliminate all instances of logical operations other than [MATH: \overline{}, \land, \lor,] then
- we rewrite the expression as a conjunction of elementary disjunctions.

In this example, we proceed as follows:

- First, we use the fact that [MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \overline{A} \lor B] to eliminate [MATH: \Rightarrow] from the expression:
[MATH: \overline{x_3} \Rightarrow (x_1 \oplus x_2)
\equiv
\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\overline{\overline{x_3}}} \lor (x_1 \oplus x_2)]
- Then, we use [MATH: \overline{\overline{A}} \equiv A] to simplify the double negation:
[MATH: \overline{\overline{x_3}} \lor (x_1 \oplus x_2)
\equiv
\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}x_3} \lor (x_1 \oplus x_2)]
- Next, we use the fact that [MATH: A \oplus B \equiv (A \lor B) \land (\overline{A} \lor \overline{B})] to eliminate [MATH: \oplus] from the expression:
[MATH: x_{3}∨(x_{1}⊕x_{2})|≡x 3∨((x 1∨x_{2})∧(x_{1}^(―)∨x 2 ―))]
- Finally, we distribute the disjunction over the conjunction:
[MATH: x_3 \lor (( x_1 \lor x_2) \land (\overline{x_1} \lor \overline{x_2}))
\equiv
(\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}x_1} \lor x_2 \lor \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}x_3}) \land (\overline{x_1} \lor \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\overline{x_2}} \lor x_3)]

Notice that the final expression is a conjunction of one or more elementary disjunctions. Therefore, this is a conjunctive normal form.
